overview.headline: Teen saving habits build emergency funds and early compound growth

keyPoints.point: Teens with steady jobs should direct at least 10 percent of earnings into their savings account.
keyPoints.quote: help them set up a savings program so that at least 10 percent of earnings goes directly into their savings account.

keyPoints.point: Emergency savings help avoid relying on credit cards or high interest loans in an emergency.
keyPoints.quote: can help your child avoid having to rely on credit cards or loan options that charge a high interest rate in case of emergency.

keyPoints.point: Starting at age 14 with $100 every year builds about $23,000 at age 65.
keyPoints.quote: If they set aside $100 every year starting at age 14, they'd have about $23,000 at age 65.

keyPoints.point: Teens offered a retirement account should save enough to earn the maximum matching contribution.
keyPoints.quote: Some employers provide matching contributions as an incentive to save, so it’s smart to save at least enough for the maximum matching contribution.

keyTerms.gloss: Automatic plan directing part of earnings into savings
keyTerms.quote: help them set up a savings program so that at least 10 percent of earnings goes directly into their savings account.

keyTerms.gloss: Monthly costs used to estimate months of emergency coverage
keyTerms.quote: have at least three months’ worth of living expenses saved up in case of an emergency.

keyTerms.gloss: Interest earned on saved money plus previously earned interest
keyTerms.quote: Compound interest is when your child earns interest on both the money they save and the interest they earn.

keyTerms.gloss: Maximum employer match earned by saving enough in a retirement account
keyTerms.quote: so it’s smart to save at least enough for the maximum matching contribution.

keyTerms.gloss: Federally insured place to keep money safe
keyTerms.quote: Talk about how to keep money in a safe place, like a federally insured bank or credit union.
